prompt: I would like to outperform the S&P 500 in the next year. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy?
reply:
# 10 Stock Ideas for the Next 12 Months

Before the list, three things affect how you should use it:

- **Beating the index is hard.** In most years, most professional US large-cap fund managers underperform the S&P 500, and over 10+ years roughly 85–90% do. Over a single year, luck matters more than skill.
- **My information is dated.** My knowledge runs through about May 2026, and I don't have live prices. Check current valuations, recent earnings and news before buying.
- **You only beat the index by being different from it.** Several of these stocks are already large S&P 500 weights. Owning them helps only if you hold more of them than the index does.

This isn't personalized advice, since I don't know your finances, time horizon or risk tolerance.

## The list

| # | Company (Ticker) | Why it could outperform | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM)** | Makes nearly all leading-edge chips, for Nvidia, Apple, AMD and others. It isn't in the S&P 500, which makes it a real differentiator. | Taiwan/China geopolitics |
| 2 | **Broadcom (AVGO)** | Custom AI chips for hyperscalers plus networking, with a sticky software business (VMware). | High valuation; depends on a few large customers |
| 3 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | Historically cheaper than its megacap peers, with a growing Google Cloud, Gemini, YouTube and Waymo. | AI disruption of Search; antitrust remedies |
| 4 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | AWS benefits from AI demand, while retail margins and advertising keep expanding. | Heavy capex weighing on free cash flow |
| 5 | **Meta Platforms (META)** | Its ad engine keeps improving with AI, and it's highly profitable. | Aggressive AI and Reality Labs spending |
| 6 | **GE Vernova (GEV)** | Rising electricity demand from data centers is driving orders for gas turbines and grid equipment. | Valuation already prices in a lot of growth |
| 7 | **Eli Lilly (LLY)** | A leader in GLP-1 obesity and diabetes drugs, including an oral pipeline. It diversifies you away from tech. | Drug pricing pressure; competition; premium valuation |
| 8 | **Intuitive Surgical (ISRG)** | Dominates robotic surgery, and recurring revenue from instruments and service grows with procedure volume. | Expensive; medtech competitors entering |
| 9 | **JPMorgan Chase (JPM)** | The best-run large bank, with a strong balance sheet and exposure to rising capital-markets activity. | Recession or credit losses |
| 10 | **Visa (V)** | Takes a cut of global card spending, with very high margins and less exposure to AI hype. | Regulation of interchange fees; slower consumer spending |

## Weaknesses of this list

- **It's largely a bet on AI.** Picks 1–6 all depend heavily on AI infrastructure spending continuing. If that spending cycle cools, much of the portfolio falls together. Picks 7–10 are there as partial balance.
- **Momentum works until it doesn't.** Many of these have already run up a lot, so a bad earnings report can hit them hard.

## How to use it

1. **Keep most of your money in the index.** A common approach is to keep 70–90% in a low-cost S&P 500 fund and put 10–30% into picks like these. You still get a chance to outperform, but a bad year won't wreck your returns.
2. **Size positions equally.** Roughly the same amount in each stock keeps one stock from dominating.
3. **Write down why you bought each one.** Decide in advance what would make you sell, such as a broken thesis or a large valuation jump, so you don't react emotionally.
4. **Check costs and taxes.** Trading fees, currency conversion, and dividend withholding taxes (if you're not a US resident) all reduce returns.
5. **Measure yourself honestly.** Compare your total return, including dividends, against an S&P 500 fund after 12 months.

I can also help you build a spreadsheet to track these against the S&P 500, compare valuation metrics once you pull current data, or stress-test a list of your own ideas.
